title: Jivaka the physician
hook: the court doctor who treated the Buddha and the monks for free

segments.voice: Yesterday, a rich man grown poor kept offering broken rice. Your line was still giving. What small gift did you make? Today, a man whose gift was medicine. Day seven hundred sixty-nine.

Is it alive? That question comes near the start of the Vinaya's account of the doctor. A newborn has been left on a rubbish heap in Rajagaha, with crows gathering around it, and a prince named Abhaya, passing by early in the morning, stops and asks. Yes, his people tell him, it's alive. So the prince has the baby carried home and raised. The text says the boy's name came from that answer: Jivaka, the one who lives. Today, the doctor that child grew up to be.
screen: `A BABY ON A RUBBISH HEAP.` → `IS IT ALIVE?` → `JIVAKA, THE ONE WHO LIVES.`

segments.voice: First, the test. Grown, Jivaka goes away to study medicine with a famous teacher. The Vinaya tells of his final exam: take a spade, walk all around the town, and bring back any plant that is not medicine. Jivaka comes back with nothing. Every plant he found, he says, could heal something. His teacher sends him home: you've learned enough to make a living. Second, the court. Back in Rajagaha he cures King Bimbisara, and the king appoints him physician to the king himself, to his household, and to the Buddha and the monks. Third, the Buddha's doctor. When the Buddha's body is out of balance, Jivaka treats him gently, the text says, with a remedy breathed in from lotus flowers. He cares for the monks so freely that, the Vinaya says, some sick men began asking to be ordained just to be treated by him. So Jivaka himself asked the Buddha not to ordain people with certain diseases, and the Buddha made that a rule. Fourth, the gifts. Jivaka gives the Buddha a pair of fine robes, and from then on monks may accept robes from householders. He has a mango grove near Rajagaha, and the Jivaka Sutta is set there; tradition says he gave it to the sangha. The baby nobody wanted becomes the man who's there when the body breaks down. And his first lesson was a field with no useless plants in it. The healer.
screen: `NO PLANT THAT ISN'T MEDICINE.` · `PHYSICIAN TO THE KING.` · `THE BUDDHA'S DOCTOR.` · `ROBES AND A MANGO GROVE.` · then, large: `THE HEALER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: care for someone's health. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person whose body is having a hard time. A parent with a bad knee. A friend just home from the hospital. A coworker who's run down. Or your own tired self. Then ask Jivaka's question from the test: what's near at hand that could help? A glass of water. A ride to an appointment. A walk together. A bedtime, kept. Choose one. Rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Jivaka the physician. Found as a baby on a rubbish heap, he became doctor to a king, to the Buddha and to the monks. Today's word.
Your line: the healer. Today, do your one small thing for someone's body, yours or theirs, with whatever's near at hand. Day seven hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Jivaka is honored in some Buddhist communities as a patron of healers; in Thailand, some traditional massage and medicine schools pay respect to him before lessons, and monasteries still receive medicine as one of the requisites lay people offer.

original.note: Pali Jivaka: the one who lives; the Vinaya ties the name to 'it's alive', said on the rubbish heap.

trapdoor: what you thought: a doctor who happened to know the Buddha.
what it means: a foundling who became healer to king, Buddha and monks, and whose care shaped the monks' rules.
what a scholar hears: his life story sits in the Mahavagga's chapter on robes, because it ends with his gift of fine robes and the Buddha allowing robes from householders.

sources.ref: Vinaya, Mahavagga 1.39 (those with certain diseases not to be ordained)

notes: Mahavagga 8.1 paraphrased. Confirm: the baby on the rubbish heap surrounded by crows; Prince Abhaya's question and the name from 'it is alive' (jivati); the teacher's test with the spade (the distance is stated in the text as a yojana; omitted); curing Bimbisara and the appointment to attend the king, the women's quarters and the Order with the Buddha at its head; the lotus remedy for the Buddha's humors; the gift of a pair of Siveyyaka cloths and the allowance of householder robes.
The study location (Takkasila) and the years of study are omitted under the claims rule.
Mahavagga 1.39: confirm that men sought ordination for Jivaka's treatment and that Jivaka asked the Buddha not to ordain those with the listed diseases.
Gift of the mango grove: confirm it is attested (MN 55 is set in Jivaka's mango grove; the formal gift is in the commentaries).
howItsDone: confirm the Thai traditional medicine and massage practice of honoring Jivaka (often as 'Father Doctor').

Editor: the account does not open with 'is it alive?' (it begins with his mother's story), so 'opens' became 'comes near the start'; the mango-grove gift (commentarial) now marked 'tradition says' in the teach and the match pair.
